strengths: Substantial and extensive benchmarking effort: SpatialScore aggregates ~28K samples from VGBench plus 11 existing datasets across 8 task categories, three QA formats, and three modalities, with a carefully constructed challenging subset (SpatialScore-Hard) selected via 20-model voting plus manual verification.

VGBench is a genuinely new contribution targeting fine-grained visual geometry perception (homography, camera intrinsics, pose, 3D reconstruction, point tracking) that is not covered by prior spatial MLLM benchmarks; the data construction pipeline (templates + distractor perturbation + LLM rewriting on datasets with accurate 3D annotations like ScanNet++, CA-1M, WildRGB-D) is described in reasonable detail in the appendix.

Very broad evaluation: 25+ open-source models spanning 1B–78B parameters plus proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0 Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku), with per-category breakdowns across multiple benchmarks and source datasets (Tables 1–10), enabling systematic analysis of scale trends, 2D vs. 3D reasoning gaps, and poor generalization of spatially fine-tuned models.

SpatialAgent is well-specified for reproducibility: all 9 tools are open-source (RAM++, OWLv2, SAM2, RAFT, SIFT/OpenCV, VGGT, DepthAnythingV2, OrientAnything), full prompt templates and tool specifications are provided in the appendix, and both Plan-Execute and ReAct paradigms are formally described.
Writing and structure are generally clear; limitations (RGB-only inputs, rudimentary toolbox) are honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: Limited scientific novelty of the main benchmark: SpatialScore is primarily a repackaging of 11 existing spatial benchmarks plus VGBench, so the core resource contribution is aggregation rather than new data; several integrated sources (e.g., ScanNet-based VSI-Bench, CV-Bench) have significant overlap with MLLM training data, and while the authors discuss ScanNet contamination for VGBench, a systematic decontamination analysis for the integrated datasets is not provided.

Question validity concerns in VGBench: several task formats are arguably testable without genuine visual reasoning (e.g., judging a numerical rotation/translation matrix, selecting a homography matrix against near-identical distractors, inferring focal length from a raw image), which risks measuring numerical/textual pattern matching rather than 'visual geometry perception'; the δ=2 tolerance (0.5×–2×) for open-ended metric answers is a very coarse correctness criterion.

Evaluation methodology for SpatialAgent has bias risks: SpatialScore-Hard is constructed by selecting samples where many MLLMs fail, and SpatialAgent is evaluated almost exclusively on this subset (Table 3) after extensive prompt engineering on SpatialScore tasks (Sec. D.3–D.4); this favors tool-augmented approaches on tool-solvable cases and offers no held-out or ablation isolating prompt engineering effects. Missing baselines include a generic ReAct agent with general-purpose tools, plain CoT, and self-consistency, so the contribution of the geometry-specific toolbox is not cleanly isolated.
Human performance is claimed ('current MLLMs still lag behind humans') but no human evaluation results are reported anywhere in the paper.

Some agent gains appear inconsistent or cherry-picked: SpatialAgent variants outperform the very models that serve as their cores by enormous margins on Hard, yet full SpatialScore results for the agent are not reported; qualitative examples in Figure 4 include agent outputs that are plainly wrong (e.g., 182 cm for a 15 cm gap, answering '8' for a stool-count question despite 'Ground Truth: A' label confusion), and textual inconsistencies exist (e.g., 60.28% vs. Table 2's 60.17% for InternVL3-78B).

The claimed distinction from prior work is partly overstated: existing benchmarks cited as 'narrow' (e.g., VSI-Bench, 3DSRBench, QSpatialBench) already cover video spatial QA, multi-object 3D reasoning, and metric estimation, so the gap SpatialScore fills is breadth/unification, which should be more precisely scoped.

Minor presentation issues: 'most comprehensive benchmark to date' is repeated many times; typos (SpaitalScore, reposenses, Cambrain); several VGBench example questions in figures reference numeric coordinates/bboxes whose visual anchoring is unclear.

strengths: Breadth of evaluation is genuinely impressive: 25 MLLMs (1B–78B, plus proprietary APIs) are evaluated under a unified, documented protocol (fixed seeds, temperature 0, tailored prompts per dataset in Appendix D.3), providing a useful reference snapshot of the field's spatial-reasoning state.

The benchmark aggregation is substantial engineering: 28K samples spanning 8 task categories, three QA formats, and single-image/multi-image/video modalities, plus a carefully constructed hard subset (16-of-20 model failure criterion plus manual verification) that is a reasonable design for a difficulty-filtered diagnostic.

The hard-subset selection methodology is described in enough detail (Appendix D.1) to be reproduced, and the paper reports honest negative results, e.g., fine-tuned spatial models (SpaceQwen2.5VL-3B, SpaceLLaVA-13B) generalize poorly, and proprietary models still score ~30% on SpatialScore-Hard.

Reproducibility support is above average for a benchmark paper: full agent prompts, tool specifications (Appendix D.4–D.5), data construction templates (Appendix D.2), and detailed per-source statistics (Tables 4–5, Figures 5–6).

Qualitative analysis (Figure 4) includes failure cases of the proposed agent, which is candid and helps diagnose when tool-augmented reasoning breaks down (e.g., confusing depth with object-to-object distance).
weaknesses: Central validity concern for VGBench: several task formats present geometric quantities (rotation matrices, translation vectors, homography matrices) as raw text in the question. A model can answer by numerical/textual manipulation rather than visual perception — e.g., the Figure 1(a) judgment example contains only text plus an image that is not obviously required. The high Pose-Est. accuracies (60–72% for large models) are consistent with a textual-arithmetic shortcut rather than 'visual geometry perception,' which undercuts the paper's headline claim of a geometry-perception benchmark. No control experiment (e.g., blind/no-image baselines) is provided to rule this out.

Limited novelty of the main contributions: 22K of the 28K SpatialScore samples are drawn from 11 existing datasets, and SpatialAgent is a fairly standard tool-orchestration system (ReAct and Plan-Execute are both established paradigms) assembling off-the-shelf models (VGGT, DepthAnythingV2, RAFT, SIFT, SAM2, OWLv2). The methodological contribution is integration, not new technique.

The agent evaluation is thin: SpatialAgent is tested only on SpatialScore-Hard with two agent cores (Qwen2.5VL-7B, InternVL-8B) and two paradigms. There is no cost/latency analysis (iterative tool calls are expensive), no per-tool ablation showing which of the 9 tools drives gains, and no results on the full SpatialScore or VGBench, so the generality of the improvement claims is not established.

The claim that MLLMs 'lag behind humans' is asserted but no human baseline is measured anywhere in the paper; the difficulty of SpatialScore-Hard for humans is unknown, particularly for matrix/pixel-coordinate tasks where the annotation source is synthetic.

Data contamination risk is acknowledged but only partially mitigated: most of SpatialScore is sourced from public benchmarks likely in training corpora, and the VGBench scenes come from ScanNet/ScanNet++/CA-1M, whose imagery may also appear in MLLM pretraining. The reliance on the δ=2 tolerance (0.5×–2×) for metric answers further inflates apparent capability.

Protocol inconsistencies vs. original benchmarks: VSI-Bench videos are uniformly subsampled to 8 frames for non-video models, and MMVP switches from question-level to sample-level accuracy; while disclosed, these deviations complicate comparison with published results and mix evaluation conventions within one aggregate score.

The abstract and text repeatedly lean on superlative framing ('most comprehensive and diverse benchmark to date') rather than analysis; the discussion of why models fail (e.g., 2D vs. 3D reasoning) is largely descriptive of the tables.

Presentation quality detracts from credibility: multiple typos ('SpaitalScore', 'reposenses', 'Cambrain', 'mutli-object', 'RealWolrdQA', 'LocalizaObjects'), and the text cites InternVL3-78B at 60.28% while Table 2 reports 60.17%.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored gap: rigorous evaluation of visual geometry perception (camera pose, homography, point tracking, 3D reconstruction) in MLLMs, which prior spatial benchmarks (VSR, SpatialSense, MMVP, etc.) largely ignore. VGBench is a concrete and novel addition in this respect.

The benchmark construction is thorough and well documented. The pipeline leverages precise 3D annotations from ScanNet, ScanNet++, CA-1M, and WildRGB-D, with carefully designed distractor generation strategies (perturbation within a margin, same-scene sampling, LLM-synthesized distractors) to prevent models from exploiting textual shortcuts — a concern the authors explicitly analyze in the appendix (e.g., the weak MMIU 3D-pose distractors).

The evaluation breadth is a major strength: 25+ models from 1B to 78B parameters plus proprietary APIs, across VGBench, SpatialScore, SpatialScore-Hard, and per-source-dataset breakdowns (Tables 6-10), with standardized decoding settings (temperature 0, fixed seeds) that support reproducibility.

SpatialScore-Hard is curated with a defensible protocol (16+ model failure voting with a large-model constraint, manual verification, category balancing), yielding a genuinely challenging subset where even GPT-4o achieves only ~30%.

SpatialAgent is built entirely from open-source expert models (VGGT, DepthAnythingV2, RAFT, OWLv2, SAM2, OrientAnything), and the appendix provides unusually complete implementation detail, including full planner/executor/summarizer prompts and per-tool specifications, which greatly aids reproduction.
The paper is honest about limitations (RGB-only inputs, rudimentary toolbox, occasional agent failures) and provides qualitative failure analysis, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: SpatialScore is primarily an aggregation of 11 existing datasets plus the new VGBench; the methodological novelty of the benchmark lies mostly in VGBench (6K samples, itself template- and LLM-generated from four existing sources). The 'most comprehensive benchmark' claim is largely about scale/integration rather than new data, and the risk that integrated datasets (e.g., ScanNet-derived subsets, BLINK, CV-Bench) are already in model training data is acknowledged but not quantitatively assessed (no decontamination analysis).

The SpatialAgent evaluation is asymmetric: the framework is tested only on the 1.4K-sample Hard subset, not on the full 28K SpatialScore, and there is no ablation isolating the contribution of individual tools, prompt engineering, or the number of agent iterations. Consequently, the attribution of gains to 'systematic tool invocation' rather than to the prompt/CoT scaffolding alone is not established — a simple CoT-only or SelfThinking-only baseline on the same subset is missing.
The repeated claim that MLLMs 'lag behind humans' is not supported by any reported human evaluation results on VGBench or SpatialScore; no human baseline table appears in the manuscript.

Some results raise data-quality questions: e.g., SpaceLLaVA-13B scores 1.00 on Tracking and 3.27 on Pose-Estimation (VGBench), and several fine-tuned spatial models collapse catastrophically on individual categories, suggesting format/instruction-following artifacts dominate parts of the ranking. The paper notes refusal/failure cases are left as-is, which conflates instruction-following with spatial ability in the aggregate 'Overall' metric.

The open-ended metric (δ=2 tolerance, i.e., within 0.5x-2x of ground truth) is coarse and inconsistent with the Mean Relative Accuracy used for VSI-Bench in its source setting; the paper's own appendix discusses this discrepancy without resolving which protocol better reflects spatial competence.

Presentation issues: text has repeated typos ('SpaitalScore', 'Cambrain', 'RealWolrdQA', 'reposenses', 'LocalizaObjects'), Figure 1/2 are dense and hard to parse, and key statistics (e.g., human performance, per-tool usage frequency, cost/latency of the two paradigms) are absent from the main text.

The two agent paradigms (Plan-Execute vs ReAct) are standard; the contribution of Sec. 3 is primarily engineering (tool wrapping and prompting) rather than a new method, and the formulation in Eqs. 1-6 is descriptive rather than analytic.
